report:
## Conclusion

The claim is **true**, not false. Strong randomized controlled trial evidence supports that exemestane reduces breast cancer incidence in postmenopausal women at elevated risk.

## Evidence

The key evidence comes from the **MAP.3 (Mammary Prevention 3) trial**, a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 3 study of 4,560 high-risk postmenopausal women, published in the *New England Journal of Medicine* (Goss et al., 2011). At a median follow-up of 35 months, exemestane (25 mg/day) reduced the incidence of invasive breast cancer by **65%** compared with placebo (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1103507). This finding was corroborated by NCI's own summary of the trial results (https://www.cancer.gov/types/breast/research/exemestane-reduces-risk) and independent secondary analyses describing the same 65% relative risk reduction (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3354700/).

Comparative chemoprevention research further situates exemestane favorably against older agents: aromatase inhibitors like exemestane appear to prevent more contralateral breast cancers and cause fewer side effects than tamoxifen, though tamoxifen and raloxifene have shown limited patient acceptance for primary prevention (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/Nejmoa1103507).

Some caveats exist: exemestane showed measurable negative effects on bone health and modest quality-of-life impacts, and researchers note that longer-term follow-up (beyond the original ~35 months) is needed to confirm durability of benefit and full safety profile. However, these caveats concern secondary effects and follow-up duration—not the core finding of reduced breast cancer incidence, which is well-established via a large, well-designed RCT.

## Bottom Line

The skepticism is unwarranted for the core claim. The MAP.3 trial, a rigorous RCT published in a top-tier journal, demonstrates a statistically significant and substantial reduction in invasive breast cancer incidence with exemestane versus placebo in exactly this population.
